Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The two hepatic lesions are limited (≤3 cm), located in segments II and V without involvement of major vascular structures, and the total tumor burden is well within the criteria for curative hepatectomy (≤5 lesions, each ≤5 cm, adequate future liver remnant expected). No extra‑hepatic disease is identified. The primary colonic tumor is symptomatic but technically resectable. Therefore both the colon primary and the liver metastases can be removed in a single operative session without the need for down‑staging therapy or additional information.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Stage the patient fully: obtain baseline labs (CBC, liver panel, coagulation, CEA), performance status (ECOG), cardiopulmonary assessment, and calculate future liver remnant volume (CT volumetry).  
• Proceed with simultaneous resection:  
   – Left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or extended left hemicolectomy) with oncologic lymphadenectomy to address the symptomatic 6 cm left‑colon tumor.  
   – Liver surgery: segment II wedge/segmentectomy (or left lateral sectionectomy if needed) and segment V anatomical resection (segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge) aiming for R0 margins while preserving ≥30 % functional liver remnant.  
• Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
• Post‑operative recovery and early mobilization; monitor liver function closely.  
• Adjuvant systemic therapy: start within 6–8 weeks after surgery. Preferred regimen is FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status, for a total of 6 months.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT volumetry) to confirm adequacy.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance if available).  
• Patient’s performance status and cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., VO₂ max, echocardiogram).  
• Detailed description of the relationship of the liver lesions to major hepatic veins/portal pedicles.  
These data are essential to finalize operative planning and to anticipate peri‑operative risk.

No extra‑hepatic disease is present, and the patient has no comorbidities that would preclude major surgery. Therefore an R0 liver resection is technically feasible without any prerequisite down‑staging or additional information.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or liver‑specific MRI) for precise mapping of the two lesions and volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant.  
   – Standard pre‑operative labs, cardiopulmonary assessment, and assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1).  
   – Discuss with anesthesia and colorectal team the plan for simultaneous surgery.  

• Surgical plan (first definitive treatment)  
   – Perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental or left hemicolectomy) to relieve the sub‑occlusive primary tumor.  
   – In the same operative session, perform limited hepatic resections: segment II resection (or wedge) and segment V resection (or wedge), achieving negative margins (R0).  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and margins; ensure preservation of inflow/outflow and biliary drainage of the remaining liver.  
   – If intra‑operative findings reveal unexpected disease burden or inadequate FLR, convert to staged approach (colon first, liver resection after recovery).  

• Post‑operative oncologic management  
   – Pathology review of primary and metastases; confirm R0 status.  
   – Initiate adjuvant systemic therapy within 6‑8 weeks: standard 6‑month FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS‑wild‑type status.  
   – Consider peri‑operative (post‑operative) chemotherapy rather than neoadjuvant, because the primary tumor required urgent resection.  
   – Follow‑up schedule: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

• Contingency options  
   – If intra‑operative assessment shows need for a major hepatectomy or FLR <30 %, plan a staged approach with portal vein embolization or two‑stage hepatectomy after recovery.  
   – If postoperative recovery is delayed, adjust timing of systemic therapy accordingly.

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential data are lacking for a reliable resectability assessment or treatment plan. The only optional information that could refine the plan is a formal volumetric calculation of the future liver remnant and baseline liver function tests (e.g., ICG clearance) to confirm adequate hepatic reserve, but these can be obtained during pre‑operative work‑up.

• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy

MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.

Reasoning: The primary ileocecal tumor is amenable to a standard right hemicolectomy. The liver lesion is a solitary 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, which can be removed with a wedge resection or limited segmentectomy while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on PET, and the patient’s performance status and organ function are not reported as limiting. Therefore both the colorectal primary and the hepatic metastasis are technically resectable without the need for down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Proceed with simultaneous curative surgery: right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy combined with a liver‑sparing resection of the segment VI metastasis (wedge or segmentectomy) using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
- Ensure negative margins (R0) on both specimens; aim for at least 1 cm margin on the liver lesion if feasible.  
- Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (6 months) with a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin backbone (FOLFOX or CAPOX), given the KRAS‑mutated tumor and elevated pre‑operative CEA, to address micrometastatic disease.  
- Schedule surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months, and colonoscopy at 1 year post‑resection.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No critical information is lacking to formulate a reliable surgical and oncologic plan; the case provides sufficient details on tumor burden, location, and metastatic status.

Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver lesion (1.8 cm, segment III) is technically resectable now, but the rectal primary (T3N1) requires neoadjuvant radiotherapy (short‑course 5 × 5 Gy) before definitive surgery. Completion of this radiotherapy (and any required systemic chemotherapy) is a prerequisite for safe curative resection of the primary, therefore the case is not “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate short‑course radiotherapy to the pelvis (5 × 5 Gy over 1 week).  
- During the interval (2–3 weeks) after radiotherapy, start peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 4 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, given RAS wild‑type) to treat micrometastatic disease and to provide a safety window for surgical planning.  
- Re‑stage with repeat pelvic MRI and liver imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI) to confirm unchanged resectability.  
- Proceed to curative surgery: perform a total mesorectal excision (TME) for the upper rectal cancer combined with a segment III liver resection (wedge or anatomical segmentectomy) in a single operative session, provided the patient’s performance status and liver function are adequate.  
- If intra‑operative assessment suggests excessive hepatic workload, consider a staged approach (liver resection first, then TME 4–6 weeks later).  
- Complete a total of 6 months of adjuvant systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (continuing FOLFOX ± targeted agent).  
- Follow‑up schedule: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelets) and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
- Cardiopulmonary fitness / ASA classification to confirm operative tolerance.  
- Detailed mesorectal fascia status (distance to MRF) and sphincter involvement to plan TME extent.  
- Chest imaging to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.

Resectable upfront  
The solitary 3 cm metastasis in segment VII is described as “deep but resectable” and no other extra‑hepatic disease is reported. The primary right colon tumor is amenable to standard oncologic resection. Assuming adequate future liver remnant (>30 % of total liver volume) and acceptable hepatic reserve, both lesions can be removed without the need for down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Assess performance status (ECOG 0‑1), baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, platelets) and calculate future liver remnant volume with CT volumetry.  
• If the patient meets operative fitness criteria, proceed with a simultaneous curative‑intent operation:  
   – Laparoscopic or open right hemicolectomy with complete mesocolic excision and central vascular ligation.  
   – Anatomical or non‑anatomical resection of segment VII (open or laparoscopic) guided by intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins; consider Pringle maneuver if needed.  
   – Ensure negative margins on both colon and liver specimens; send liver margin for frozen section if uncertainty.  
• Post‑operative management:  
   – Start adjuvant systemic therapy within 6‑8 weeks (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, given RAS wild‑type).  
   – Continue for 6 months; monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑4 months for the first 2 years.  
• If intra‑operative assessment reveals insufficient future liver remnant or unexpected vascular involvement, convert to a staged approach: first colon resection, then portal vein embolization (if needed) followed by delayed liver resection after hypertrophy.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Exact performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
• Detailed liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance or similar hepatic reserve assessment.  
• Volumetric measurement of future liver remnant.  
• Precise T and N stage of the colon primary (depth of invasion, nodal involvement).  
• Presence or absence of additional extra‑hepatic lesions (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
• Comorbidities that could affect surgical risk (cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, etc.).  
These data are essential to confirm operative fitness and to fine‑tune the peri‑operative plan.

Therefore the case meets criteria for “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Full liver function panel (bilirubin, INR, albumin, AST/ALT) and indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm adequate hepatic reserve.  
   – Volumetric CT or MRI to calculate future liver remnant; aim for ≥30 % in a healthy liver.  
   – Staging chest CT/PET‑CT to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary fitness.  

• Surgical plan (simultaneous resection)  
   1. Laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with oncologic (mesocolic) resection and primary anastomosis (or diverting stoma if needed).  
   2. Left hepatectomy (anatomic resection of segments II‑IV) performed immediately after colon resection; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion number, size, and margins.  
   3. Aim for R0 margins (>1 cm when feasible) on both colon and liver specimens.  
   4. Meticulous hemostasis and bile‑duct management; consider Pringle maneuver ≤15 min total ischemia.  

• Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Initiate adjuvant FOLFOX (or CAPOX) for 6 months, beginning 4‑6 weeks after surgery, provided adequate recovery.  
   – KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents; consider adding bevacizumab only if high‑risk features (e.g., multiple nodes, poor differentiation) and wound‑healing risk is acceptable (delay ≥6 weeks).  
   – Monitor CEA every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years.  

• Contingency  
   – If intra‑operative assessment reveals insufficient FLR, convert to staged approach: perform colon resection first, then portal vein embolization of the right portal branch followed by delayed left hepatectomy.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative liver function and volumetry (future liver remnant percentage).  
• Detailed performance status and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the left lobe (full chest imaging, PET‑CT if not already done).  
• Baseline laboratory values (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) to assess surgical risk.  

These data are essential to finalize operative planning and to ensure patient safety.
